original_value: Latent heat flux (LE) and the corresponding water vapor lost from the Earth’s surface to the atmosphere, which is called Evapotranspiration (ET), is one of the key processes in the water cycle and energy balance of the global climate system. Satellite remote sensing is the only feasible technique to estimate LE over a large-scale region. While most of the previous satellite LE methods are based on the optical vegetation index (VI), here we propose a microwave-VI (EDVI) based LE algorithm which can work for both day and night time, and under clear or non-raining conditions. This algorithm is totally driven by multiple-sensor satellite products of vegetation water content index, solar radiation, and cloud properties, with some aid from a reanalysis dataset. The satellite inputs and the performance of this algorithm are validated with in situ measurements at three ChinaFLUX forest sites. Our results show that the selected satellite observations can indeed serve as the inputs for the purpose of estimating ET. The instantaneous estimations of LE (LEcal) from this algorithm show strong positive temporal correlations with the in situ measured LE (LEobs) with the correlation coefficients (R) of 0.56–0.88 in the study years. The mean bias is kept within 16.0% (23.0 W/m2) across the three sites. At the monthly scale, the correlations between the retrieval and the in situ measurements are further improved to an R of 0.84–0.95 and the bias is less than 14.3%. The validation results also indicate that EDVI-based LE method can produce stable LEcal under different cloudy skies with good accuracy. Being independent of any in situ measurements as inputs, this algorithm shows great potential for estimating ET under both clear and cloudy skies on a global scale for climate study.

result.paraphrase: Latent heat flux (LE), along with the water vapor transferred from the Earth’s surface to the atmosphere through evapotranspiration (ET), is a key component of the water cycle and the energy balance in the global climate system. Satellite remote sensing is the only practical way to estimate LE over large regions. Although most earlier satellite-based LE approaches rely on optical vegetation indices (VI), we present a microwave-VI (EDVI)-based LE algorithm that operates during both day and night and under clear or non-raining conditions. The method is driven entirely by multisensor satellite products for vegetation water content index, solar radiation, and cloud properties, with some support from a reanalysis dataset. Satellite inputs and algorithm performance are validated against in situ observations at three ChinaFLUX forest sites. The results demonstrate that the selected satellite observations can serve as effective inputs for ET estimation. Instantaneous LE estimates (LEcal) from the algorithm are strongly and positively correlated with in situ LE measurements (LEobs), with correlation coefficients (R) of 0.56–0.88 in the study years. Mean bias remains within 16.0% (23.0 W/m2) across the three sites. At the monthly scale, agreement improves further, with R rising to 0.84–0.95 and bias below 14.3%. Validation also shows that the EDVI-based LE method can generate stable and accurate LEcal under varying cloudy conditions. Because it does not require any in situ measurements as inputs, the algorithm has strong potential for global ET estimation under both clear and cloudy skies for climate studies.
